stories.title: Gemini VIII, part 1: the first docking, then the roll
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: loved Apollo 13 the film and The Right Stuff. This is the near miss that came before them, with Neil Armstrong in the seat.
Facts: March 16, 1966. Gemini VIII, command pilot Neil Armstrong, pilot David Scott.
The job was the first docking in space, joining their capsule to an Agena target vehicle. Apollo needed that technique to get to the Moon.
They did it: the world's first space docking.
Twenty-seven minutes later, while the Agena turned the joined craft 90 degrees, Scott noticed they were also rolling.
Armstrong used the Gemini's thrusters to stop it. It stopped, then started again and got worse: a roll and a tumble together.
They were out of touch with Houston, far from any tracking station. They couldn't see the panel properly and were afraid the Agena might break apart and blow up.
They decided the Agena was to blame, so Scott hit the undock button.
Hook: that call made sense with what they knew, and it was wrong. What happened once they let go comes later.

stories.topic: Jazz: the players, how the records were made, what to listen to next
stories.title: Kind of Blue: all first takes?
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: Kind of Blue is one of their five-star albums.
The belief to ask: Miles Davis recorded all of Kind of Blue in one pass, with every track a first take. Myth or fact?
The setup, facts only: two sessions at Columbia's 30th Street Studio in New York, March 2 and April 22, 1959.
Davis called for almost no rehearsal. The band got only sketches of scales and melody lines.
Point: ask it plainly and leave it with them. The answer comes a rest later.

stories.topic: Space history: the missions, the people, the near misses
stories.title: Gemini VIII, part 2: the stuck thruster
stories.text:
Where we were: Armstrong and Scott had just undocked from the Agena, which they thought was the problem.
The turn: once they were free, the spin got worse. The fault was on their own ship. Thruster No. 8 had short-circuited and stuck on.
When they reached the tracking ship Coastal Sentry Quebec, Scott's call: "We have serious problems here." Then "We're tumbling, end over end."
The spin reached 60 revolutions per minute. Checklists flew around the cabin and sunlight strobed through the windows. Both men came close to blacking out.
Armstrong's fix: he shut off the main thruster system and fought the spin with the Reentry Control System, the thrusters in the nose that were meant for coming home.
It worked, but it used three-quarters of that propellant. Mission rules meant they had to come home right away. They splashed down in the western Pacific.
Scott later: "The guy was brilliant. He knew the system so well."
Take: they lost the rest of the mission but saved the crew, and the docking still counted. Forty months later Armstrong commanded Apollo 11.
Hook for next time: in July 1966 Michael Collins flew over to that same abandoned Agena and finished a job Gemini VIII had to leave behind.

stories.topic: Jazz: the players, how the records were made, what to listen to next
stories.title: Kind of Blue: the answer
stories.text:
Answer: mostly myth. Wikipedia calls the one-pass legend untrue.
Why it sticks: Bill Evans's own liner notes said he thought the first complete performance of each piece was a take.
What the tapes show: on take 3 of "Freddie Freeloader", Davis whistled off the take during Wynton Kelly's solo. He was still making small changes.
There's also a complete alternate take of "Flamenco Sketches".
Detail: the whole thing fits on three reels of tape.
Point: Davis kept the music loose but the structure strict, and he would stop a take over one missed turn.

stories.topic: Jazz: the players, how the records were made, what to listen to next
stories.title: Sunday at the Village Vanguard
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: the pianist on Kind of Blue is Bill Evans, and this is the record he made next with his own trio.
What it is: a live album by the Bill Evans Trio, with Scott LaFaro on bass and Paul Motian on drums. It was recorded on June 25, 1961, at the Village Vanguard in New York.
They played five sets that day.
The detail: LaFaro died in a car accident ten days after the recording, so the album became something of a tribute to him. His bass playing is out front.
AllMusic calls it a great place to begin with Evans.
When: a calm evening in the hotel room, from start to finish.

stories.topic: Space history: the missions, the people, the near misses
stories.title: Why the Great Wall disappears from orbit
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: a myth about space that people still repeat.
The question: the Great Wall is huge, so why can't astronauts see it?
The one idea: the eye picks things out by contrast, not by size. The wall is narrow, and its stone and clay are about the same color as the ground around it.
Astronaut Jeffrey Hoffman flew five shuttle missions and never saw it: "the human eye is most sensitive to contrast."
He could pick out roads, runways and irrigation ditches because they stand out from what's around them.
The Moon claim goes back to a 1932 Ripley's Believe It or Not! cartoon. NASA says the wall isn't visible from the Moon, and it's hard or impossible to see from orbit without strong lenses.
Point to repeat: from space, what shows up is what stands out from its background, not what's biggest.

stories.title: Squats where nothing weighs anything
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: space history, and Jo trains in a small room with almost no kit, like a crew on the station.
The problem: without Earth's gravity, bone and muscle shrink and weaken. For every month in space, astronauts' weight-bearing bones become roughly 1% less dense if they don't take precautions.
The training: crews on the space station average two hours of exercise a day.
Their lifting machine, ARED, installed in 2008, uses a piston and flywheel to mimic weightlifting in weightlessness.
Astronaut Michael Lopez-Alegria on why it's mostly legs: 'my shoes look pretty clean on the bottom because they've never really stepped on anything.' So they do a lot of squats and deadlifts, single-leg and two-leg squats.
NASA also found shorter, harder workouts did about as well as long easy ones and saved crew time.
Link to this set: the legs and spine are what carry you on Earth, so they get the work first. A small space and a short session still count.

stories.title: Apollo 13: the answer
stories.text:
Where we were: who first radioed the problem, and was it 'we have a problem'?
Answer: Jack Swigert, not Lovell: 'Okay, Houston, we've had a problem here.'
Capcom Jack Lousma: 'This is Houston. Say again, please.'
Then Lovell: 'Ah, Houston, we've had a problem. We've had a Main B Bus Undervolt.'
So it was 'we've had', not 'we have'. The Apollo 13 Flight Journal says the film's writers admitted they used the line viewers expected, for the sake of drama.
The fun bit: in the film Kevin Bacon plays Swigert, but the famous line goes to Tom Hanks as Lovell.
Point: the real call was calmer and more exact. It reported what had already happened and what the panel showed, a good habit in a crisis.

stories.title: Coltrane's silent practice
stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: John Coltrane plays tenor sax on Kind of Blue, one of their five-star albums. This also ties to a hotel room where you keep the noise down.
The person: from his early teens Coltrane kept up an intense practice routine and played for hours each day.
The detail: when neighbors complained, he silently fingered the keys of his saxophone late into the night, without blowing any air.
His first wife, Naima, called him 'ninety-percent saxophone'.
He worked through practice books like Nicolas Slonimsky's Thesaurus of Scales and Melodic Patterns.
Biographer Lewis Porter, as quoted in a Colby thesis, says the silent fingering was good practice for hearing the music in one's head, which improvising needs.
Link to this set: no loud reps and no big kit, just the pattern done exactly and over again until it's automatic. Quiet work still builds the skill.

stories.text:
Why it's Jo's: they gave Apollo Thirteen the film five and The Right Stuff the book four. This is the book the film came from, and it follows the quiz answer about the misquote.
What it is: Lost Moon: The Perilous Voyage of Apollo 13, by Jim Lovell and journalist Jeffrey Kluger, published 1994. In paperback it's called Apollo 13.
It's the basis of the 1995 Ron Howard film starring Tom Hanks as Lovell.
Kluger first approached Lovell about the book in 1991.
The detail: it's written in matter-of-fact third person. Lovell said the film used artistic license: it played up a confrontation between Haise and Swigert, and the opening party scene was made up.
When: the next flight home for work, to see which scenes really happened.

Jo, welcome to our first session. I'm Coach Freya. Tuesday, fifteen minutes of hotel-room strength at about a six out of ten: a quick warm-up, three rounds of glute bridges, incline push-ups and towel door rows, then a cool-down.

You'll need a sturdy chair against a wall, a towel, a solid inside door, and carpet or a folded towel.

Your left knee stays light today. Only as deep as it's comfortable, no jumping, and a pinch at the front or a catch means stop that move. An ache around two or three out of ten is fine. Sharp pain or new swelling, stop that move.

Numbness, tingling, dizziness or a joint giving way, we're done for today. Chest pain or pressure, feeling faint, or a racing or pounding heart, stop the session and get help.

AI built this, not a certified trainer or a clinician, so your judgment and your doctor come first.

Marching in place, forty seconds, easy. Stand tall, feet under your hips, arms loose. Your left knee lifts only as high as feels easy and tracks over your toes. A pinch or a catch, stop. [count 3 go]

Soft, quiet feet, opposite arm swinging, chatting pace.

Jo, here's a near miss from before Apollo Thirteen.

[story]March nineteen sixty-six, Gemini Eight. Neil Armstrong and David Scott pulled off the world's first docking in space. Twenty-seven minutes later they were rolling, then tumbling, far from Houston.

They blamed the target vehicle, so Scott hit undock. It made sense. It was wrong.[/story]

More later. Last ten seconds, then arm circles, sitting or standing.

Arm circles, twenty-five seconds, seated or standing. Arms out at shoulder height, small circles growing bigger, shoulders down. If a shoulder pinches, go smaller. [count 3 go]

Small and smooth, building bigger.

Halfway now, reverse the direction.

Shoulders low, breathing easy. [hold]

And rest. Onto the floor for bridges, carpet or a towel under your back. About ten seconds.

Glute bridge, fifteen reps, three left in the tank. On your back, knees bent, feet hip width. Ribs down, lift till knees to shoulders make a line, squeeze, lower slowly.

Feel it in the hips, not the low back. For a sore knee, hip work along with knee work does more than knee work alone. [count 3 go] [reps 15] Lift and squeeze. [hold 5s] Back arching? Ribs down, stop sooner. [hold 5s] Knees hip width. [hold 5s] Squeeze at the top. [hold 5s] Last few, slow down. [hold 5s]

And rest.

One slow breath out. Clean with three or more left? Hold steady next time. Knee grumble, smaller lift. Unsure, hold steady.

Jo, a Kind of Blue one.

[story]Miles Davis recorded the whole album in one pass, every track a first take. Two sessions in New York, spring nineteen fifty-nine, almost no rehearsal, just sketches of scales and melodies. True or not?[/story]

Answer next rest. Up and over to the chair.

Incline push-up, forty seconds, steady, finishing with two or three left. Hands on the chair edge, chair firm against the wall, then walk your feet back until you're one long line from head to heels.

Lower your chest to the edge, push the chair away, and move in one piece. Feel it in your chest, the fronts of your shoulders and the backs of your arms. If your hips sag, squeeze your glutes and brace. [count 3 go]

Down smooth, push the chair away.

I get picky here, Jo. One clean stroke beats three messy ones. Count the clean ones.

Halfway now. Breathe out as you push.

If the last two felt clean, that's the standard.

Last ten seconds. Elbows at a gentle angle, not flared out. [hold]

And rest.

Long breath out. Easy? Feet further back next time. A grind? Hands on the wall. Unsure, go a step harder.

That Kind of Blue question.

[story]Mostly myth. Bill Evans's own liner notes started it, but on take three of Freddie Freeloader, Davis whistled the take off mid-solo, still making changes.

Loose music, strict structure, and the whole album fits on three reels of tape. I love that.[/story]

To the door. Solid, inside, opens away, latched. Towel round the handle.

Towel door row, forty seconds, two or three left at the end. Inside door only, never the entry door, opening away from you and latched.

Towel round the handle, an end in each hand, lean back with your arms long.

Pull your chest to your hands, body in one line, lower back out with control. Feel it in the middle of your back and the backs of your shoulders.

Hips sag, squeeze your glutes. If the door shifts at all, stop and check the latch. [count 3 go]

Pull in, and ease back out.

My favorite in the room, Jo. The rowing stroke without the boat. Smooth beats fast.

Halfway now. Breathe out as you pull.

Last ten seconds. Shoulders down, elbows back, no shrug. [hold]

And rest. Let the towel go.

Breathe out. Easy? Feet closer to the door, steeper lean. Too much, step back and stand taller. Unsure, go steeper.

Here's a space myth.

[story]Why can't astronauts see the Great Wall? The eye picks things out by contrast, not size, and the wall is narrow and the color of the ground around it.

Jeffrey Hoffman flew five shuttle missions and never saw it, yet he could spot runways.[/story]

Down to the floor for bridges.

Glute bridge, second set, fifteen reps, same height. Hold a beat at the top. [count 3 go] [reps 15] Lift, squeeze, lower. [hold 7s] Beat at the top. [hold 7s] Ribs down now. [hold 7s] Last few, smooth. [hold 7s]

And rest.

Breathe out. Round one banked, round two under way.

A question from Apollo Thirteen, one of your five-star films.

[story]Jim Lovell, Jack Swigert and Fred Haise. Fifty-five hours into the flight, a dull bang runs through the spacecraft. Which of the three was first to radio Houston?

And were the words really Houston, we have a problem? So, which one called it in first?[/story]

Answer in two rests. Up to the chair, your push-up setup.

Glute bridge, last set, fifteen reps, three or more left. Lower in notches. [count 3 go] [reps 15] Lift and squeeze. [hold 7s] Lower in notches. [hold 7s] Stay smooth now. [hold 7s] Slow all the way down. [hold 7s]

And rest.

Breathe out. Bridges done.

Small room, almost no kit, Jo, like a space station crew.

[story]Up there, bone and muscle weaken, weight-bearing bones losing about one percent of their density a month without precautions. So crews average two hours of exercise a day, much of it legs.

As one astronaut put it, his shoes stay clean on the bottom, they've never really stepped on anything.[/story]

Up to the chair for the last push-ups.

Box breathing, forty seconds. Lie back or sit tall, shoulders dropped. In for four, hold four, out four, hold four. Belly moves, shoulders still. If the holds feel tight, make it three. [count 3 go]

Breathe in slowly, filling the belly.

Hold it there, nice and still.

Out through the mouth, slow and even.

And hold, shoulders soft.

Once more, in through the nose.

Hold it there.

Long, slow breath out.

Hold, then let it go. [hold]

First session done, Jo. Nine sets, three rounds, in the bank. Next time, Gemini has one more chapter. How hard did today feel, out of ten?
